reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript presents a system for electrochemical direct air capture (eDAC) using a novel pyridine derivative, 2,5-bis(4-pyridyl)-1,3,4-thiadiazole (BPT), in conjunction with a gas permeation layer (GPL) to mitigate oxygen-induced parasitic reactions. While the conceptual framework is timely and relevant for CO₂ separation, I cannot recommend the manuscript in its current form. The central claims—particularly regarding robustness and long-term electrochemical stability—are not adequately supported by the data. Below are my major revision points.
1. Choice and Justification of BPT
The rationale for selecting BPT is underdeveloped. Many alternatives exist for electron-withdrawing substituents or conjugation-extended pyridines. The thiadiazole ring is relatively uncommon and should be justified with comparative data or literature precedent. A brief discussion of its electronic influence (e.g., quantified via Hammett σ constants or electrochemical comparisons) would help contextualize this choice.
2. Insufficient Evidence for Oxygen Tolerance
The central claim of O₂ stability is primarily supported by a single CV trace (Fig. 1f), which only probes short timescales. No time-dependent electrochemical or spectroscopic data are provided to demonstrate long-term stability or suppression of oxidative degradation. Additional studies, such as repeated cycling under O₂, are necessary to substantiate robustness. Furthermore, Figure 1f visually obscures the blue traces under red ones, making it difficult to independently assess O₂ influence. Please clarify the visual presentation and provide quantifiable comparisons.
3. Mechanistic Evidence for CO₂ Binding Site and Stability
The mechanistic proposal hinges on selective CO₂ binding at the pyridine nitrogen of BPT, yet this is supported only indirectly via in situ IR and DFT. No direct structural or spectroscopic evidence (e.g., NMR, HRMS, isotopic labeling) is presented to confirm the identity or reversibility of the CO₂ adduct.
- Line 92: Equal anodic and cathodic peak currents do not imply thermodynamic stability; please revise this interpretation.
- Line 144: Figure S1 shows diminished current over 50 cycles, contradicting the claim of 'high reversibility.'
- Line 206: Please elaborate on how charge delocalization leads to reduced O₂ sensitivity—this concept is mentioned but not explained.
In addition, Figure 1h shows divergent UV–vis behavior depending on the CO₂ exposure sequence, suggesting additional pathways or side reactions not accounted for in the proposed mechanism. Further mechanistic validation would significantly strengthen the manuscript.
Several other figures (e.g., S1, 1e, 1h) imply degradation or irreversible processes that contradict claims of 'sustained reversibility.' Please moderate language accordingly and re-evaluate your interpretation of electrochemical reversibility. I cannot be convinced its stability by the presented data.
4. Discussion of Energy Metrics Lacks Clarity
The distinction between total energy consumption (kJ) and normalized energy consumption (kJ mol⁻¹ CO₂) is not clearly delineated in the main text (line 138). This leads to potential confusion when interpreting system performance. Please restructure this discussion to explicitly distinguish device-level and molecular-level energy metrics.
5. Figure Organization and Captioning
The presentation of Figure 1 is confusing: panels c and d could be merged, and the caption order does not align with panel labels. Reorganizing these figures will improve clarity and prevent misinterpretation.
6. No essential concentration was demonstrated.
Figure 4d and f does not show any concentration than the feed gas. Additional experimental demonstration of “concentration” should be included.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this work, Hou et al. report a redox-swing direct-air-capture (eDAC) technology that uses an extended-conjugation bipyridine, 2,5-bis(4-pyridyl)-1,3,4-thiadiazole (BPT), coupled with a Pebax-based gas-permeation layer (GPL). They start with different aromatic functionalization and narrow it down to BPT because of its superior performance compared to the other functionalized aromatics that they tested. The mechanism they highlight is the reduction of BPT binds CO2 to form a reversible di-anionic adduct reduces at –1.64 V vs Fc/Fc⁺, binds CO₂ to form a reversible BPT2- adduct. When spray-deposited (≈10 mg) on carbon paper, delivers 1.6 mmol g⁻¹BPT capture capacity at 1000 ppm CO₂ with 39 % electron efficiency and 162 kJ mol⁻¹ energy input after energy-recovery assumptions. Embedding BPT behind a 0.2 mg cm⁻² Pebax layer suppresses O₂ crossover (CO₂/O₂ permeability ratio 6.2/1.1= 5.6) and enables 36 cycles in ambient air (400 ppm CO₂, 21 % O₂) with 1.1 mmol g⁻¹BPT capacity, ~30 % electron utilization and 181 kJ mol⁻¹ energy input. In situ IR and DFT indicate that CO₂ binds preferentially to the pyridyl N’s, following an ECE mechanism. While this new chemistry is convincingly demonstrated, the practical relevance of the metrics, particularly under humid, O₂-rich conditions and over extended duty cycles, may be validated better or at least the conclusions around that could be bound a bit more. I have highlighted my concerns below that I believe the authors can address to make their work more robust:
Major points:
1. True DAC operating window: There are limited testing at 400 ppm to call it a “true DAC” for the most part. All performance claims are made at 1000 ppm or in short (15 min) batch captures from static air. Can the authors comment on how their system could handle continuous flow tests at 400 ppm? Could the authors comment on the systems durability in such a case?
2. Humidity tolerance: BPT was tested in DMSO with ≤10 vol % H₂O, yet atmospheric air can reach 30–80 % RH. Have the authors tested their system with CVs and cycling at ≥50 % RH (or with an aqueous/IL blend electrolyte) are necessary to validate stability. Or do the authors justify that they would use this technology by drying the feed gas at deployment?
3. Balance faradaic efficiency: We see the electron utilization or faradaic efficiency of the process remains less than 40% even with pure CO2 feed. And it becomes lower when the CO2 concentration is lowered. What are the rest of the electrons doing? Do we have an account or estimate for the other parasitic reactions? What would the authors propose mitigating these other parasitic reactions?
4. Material stability and lifetime: It would be nice to see if the authors can give a characterization (NMR, XPS etc if possible) of the materials, electrodes, electrolyte before and after long cycles to provide evidence that the Pebax and BPT don’t degrade significantly.
5. Mass-normalized capacity reporting: Beauty is in the eye of the denominator. Right now the capacity is reported normalized to BPT mass. Typically, in an electrochemical process, it is always economically relevant to have these things reported normalized to electrode mass or area and specific the BPT loading/distribution. They already have a nice table S2 in the SI and perhaps these additional data points can be added there.
6. Error bars: are these all one-off experiments? Or the data reported the average values of multiple runs. If they have error bars, I strongly encourage them to report it.
Minor
1. Computational methodology: are DFT free energies reported without ZPE corrections? Could the authors supply these details and confirm that implicit-solvent parameters reflect DMSO electrolyte?
2. On page 15, do the authors mean Fig 4 when they mention Fig 3 (specifically 4d and e when they say 3d and e)
3. Energy consumption reported as kJ/mol of CO2 is it per mol CO2 captured or released? Are they the same?
4. Gas flow rate and Reynolds number in methods would be a nice addition. Are they the same conditions used to calibrate the CO2 sensor? Is the CO2 sensor dependent on flowrate?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors investigate the electrochemical direct air capture (DAC) performance of 2,5-bis(4-pyridyl)-1,3,4-thiadiazole (BPT) as a redox-active material. The inclusion of pyridine groups and extended conjugation appears to enhance the molecule’s oxidative stability and CO₂ uptake capacity. Additionally, the authors use a thin-film membrane layer to mitigate O₂ permeation into the bulk region, which was suggested to improve stability.
However, while these modifications offer benefits, they may also introduce significant mass transport limitations for CO₂. The authors themselves acknowledge reduced sorption kinetics, which I believe are primarily due to the presence of the membrane layer, potentially acting as a barrier to CO₂ diffusion. Overall, while I find the work to be interesting and potentially valuable, it currently lacks sufficient depth for publication in Nature Communications. '
I have a few specific concerns and suggestions:
Were the gas permeation tests conducted under humid conditions? If not, the data may not accurately reflect real-world scenarios. The swelling of the membrane under humid conditions could significantly increase O₂ permeance, leading to misleading conclusions if this effect is not accounted for.
While the authors examine the effect of H₂O, it appears that oxidative degradation under combined O₂ and humidity conditions was not evaluated. Given that real DAC systems operate in ambient air with varying humidity, it is essential to assess stability under all relevant conditions. Previous studies have suggested that humidity can accelerate degradation processes.
The conditions under which the data in Figures 4d and 4f were collected need to be clearly described. What gas mixtures, relative humidity (RH%), and flow rates were used? This information is critical for evaluating the relevance and reproducibility of the reported results.

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript presents a system for electrochemical direct air capture (eDAC) using a novel pyridine derivative, 2,5-bis(4-pyridyl)-1,3,4-thiadiazole (BPT), in conjunction with a gas permeation layer (GPL) to mitigate oxygen-induced parasitic reactions. While the conceptual framework is timely and relevant for CO₂ separation, I cannot recommend the manuscript in its current form. The central claims—particularly regarding robustness and long-term electrochemical stability—are not adequately supported by the data. Below are my major revision points.
1. Choice and Justification of BPT
The rationale for selecting BPT is underdeveloped. Many alternatives exist for electron-withdrawing substituents or conjugation-extended pyridines. The thiadiazole ring is relatively uncommon and should be justified with comparative data or literature precedent. A brief discussion of its electronic influence (e.g., quantified via Hammett σ constants or electrochemical comparisons) would help contextualize this choice.
2. Insufficient Evidence for Oxygen Tolerance
The central claim of O₂ stability is primarily supported by a single CV trace (Fig. 1f), which only probes short timescales. No time-dependent electrochemical or spectroscopic data are provided to demonstrate long-term stability or suppression of oxidative degradation. Additional studies, such as repeated cycling under O₂, are necessary to substantiate robustness. Furthermore, Figure 1f visually obscures the blue traces under red ones, making it difficult to independently assess O₂ influence. Please clarify the visual presentation and provide quantifiable comparisons.
3. Mechanistic Evidence for CO₂ Binding Site and Stability
The mechanistic proposal hinges on selective CO₂ binding at the pyridine nitrogen of BPT, yet this is supported only indirectly via in situ IR and DFT. No direct structural or spectroscopic evidence (e.g., NMR, HRMS, isotopic labeling) is presented to confirm the identity or reversibility of the CO₂ adduct.

- Line 144: Figure S1 shows diminished current over 50 cycles, contradicting the claim of 'high reversibility.'

### Reviewer 2

In this work, Hou et al. report a redox-swing direct-air-capture (eDAC) technology that uses an extended-conjugation bipyridine, 2,5-bis(4-pyridyl)-1,3,4-thiadiazole (BPT), coupled with a Pebax-based gas-permeation layer (GPL). They start with different aromatic functionalization and narrow it down to BPT because of its superior performance compared to the other functionalized aromatics that they tested. The mechanism they highlight is the reduction of BPT binds CO2 to form a reversible di-anionic adduct reduces at –1.64 V vs Fc/Fc⁺, binds CO₂ to form a reversible BPT2- adduct. When spray-deposited (≈10 mg) on carbon paper, delivers 1.6 mmol g⁻¹BPT capture capacity at 1000 ppm CO₂ with 39 % electron efficiency and 162 kJ mol⁻¹ energy input after energy-recovery assumptions. Embedding BPT behind a 0.2 mg cm⁻² Pebax layer suppresses O₂ crossover (CO₂/O₂ permeability ratio 6.2/1.1= 5.6) and enables 36 cycles in ambient air (400 ppm CO₂, 21 % O₂) with 1.1 mmol g⁻¹BPT capacity, ~30 % electron utilization and 181 kJ mol⁻¹ energy input. In situ IR and DFT indicate that CO₂ binds preferentially to the pyridyl N’s, following an ECE mechanism. While this new chemistry is convincingly demonstrated, the practical relevance of the metrics, particularly under humid, O₂-rich conditions and over extended duty cycles, may be validated better or at least the conclusions around that could be bound a bit more. I have highlighted my concerns below that I believe the authors can address to make their work more robust:
Major points:
1. True DAC operating window: There are limited testing at 400 ppm to call it a “true DAC” for the most part. All performance claims are made at 1000 ppm or in short (15 min) batch captures from static air. Can the authors comment on how their system could handle continuous flow tests at 400 ppm? Could the authors comment on the systems durability in such a case?
2. Humidity tolerance: BPT was tested in DMSO with ≤10 vol % H₂O, yet atmospheric air can reach 30–80 % RH. Have the authors tested their system with CVs and cycling at ≥50 % RH (or with an aqueous/IL blend electrolyte) are necessary to validate stability. Or do the authors justify that they would use this technology by drying the feed gas at deployment?
3. Balance faradaic efficiency: We see the electron utilization or faradaic efficiency of the process remains less than 40% even with pure CO2 feed. And it becomes lower when the CO2 concentration is lowered. What are the rest of the electrons doing? Do we have an account or estimate for the other parasitic reactions? What would the authors propose mitigating these other parasitic reactions?
4. Material stability and lifetime: It would be nice to see if the authors can give a characterization (NMR, XPS etc if possible) of the materials, electrodes, electrolyte before and after long cycles to provide evidence that the Pebax and BPT don’t degrade significantly.
5. Mass-normalized capacity reporting: Beauty is in the eye of the denominator. Right now the capacity is reported normalized to BPT mass. ### Reviewer 3

The authors investigate the electrochemical direct air capture (DAC) performance of 2,5-bis(4-pyridyl)-1,3,4-thiadiazole (BPT) as a redox-active material. The inclusion of pyridine groups and extended conjugation appears to enhance the molecule’s oxidative stability and CO₂ uptake capacity. Additionally, the authors use a thin-film membrane layer to mitigate O₂ permeation into the bulk region, which was suggested to improve stability.
However, while these modifications offer benefits, they may also introduce significant mass transport limitations for CO₂. The authors themselves acknowledge reduced sorption kinetics, which I believe are primarily due to the presence of the membrane layer, potentially acting as a barrier to CO₂ diffusion. Overall, while I find the work to be interesting and potentially valuable, it currently lacks sufficient depth for publication in Nature Communications. '
I have a few specific concerns and suggestions:
Were the gas permeation tests conducted under humid conditions? If not, the data may not accurately reflect real-world scenarios. The swelling of the membrane under humid conditions could significantly increase O₂ permeance, leading to misleading conclusions if this effect is not accounted for.
While the authors examine the effect of H₂O, it appears that oxidative degradation under combined O₂ and humidity conditions was not evaluated. Given that real DAC systems operate in ambient air with varying humidity, it is essential to assess stability under all relevant conditions. Previous studies have suggested that humidity can accelerate degradation processes.
The conditions under which the data in Figures 4d and 4f were collected need to be clearly described. What gas mixtures, relative humidity (RH%), and flow rates were used? This information is critical for evaluating the relevance and reproducibility of the reported results.

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript presents a system for electrochemical direct air capture (eDAC) using a novel pyridine derivative, 2,5-bis(4-pyridyl)-1,3,4-thiadiazole (BPT), in conjunction with a gas permeation layer (GPL) to mitigate oxygen-induced parasitic reactions. While the conceptual framework is timely and relevant for CO₂ separation, I cannot recommend the manuscript in its current form. The central claims—particularly regarding robustness and long-term electrochemical stability—are not adequately supported by the data. Below are my major revision points.
1. Choice and Justification of BPT
The rationale for selecting BPT is underdeveloped. Many alternatives exist for electron-withdrawing substituents or conjugation-extended pyridines. The thiadiazole ring is relatively uncommon and should be justified with comparative data or literature precedent. A brief discussion of its electronic influence (e.g., quantified via Hammett σ constants or electrochemical comparisons) would help contextualize this choice.
2. Insufficient Evidence for Oxygen Tolerance
The central claim of O₂ stability is primarily supported by a single CV trace (Fig. 1f), which only probes short timescales. No time-dependent electrochemical or spectroscopic data are provided to demonstrate long-term stability or suppression of oxidative degradation. Please clarify the visual presentation and provide quantifiable comparisons.
